title: Optical switching of antiferromagnetic domains by nonreciprocal heat current
authors: Takeshi Hayashida, Shunsuke Izumikawa, Kenta Kimura, Carl S. Davies, Andrei Kirilyuk
abstract: What distinguishes front from back? In physics, such directionality emerges only when an underlying symmetry is broken. Antiferromagnets that inherently break both space-inversion and time-reversal symmetries provide a striking example, exhibiting nonreciprocal optical responses that depend on the direction of light propagation. Beyond distinguishing antiferromagnetic domains, we show that this nonreciprocity can deterministically create them. Using mid-infrared light, we demonstrate deterministic switching of antiferromagnetic domains in the magnetoelectric antiferromagnet LiFePO4, where illumination from opposite sides selectively stabilizes opposite domain states. Remarkably, the switching persists over a broad wavelength range rather than being confined to a narrow transition-specific spectral region, overcoming the spectral and material constraints of resonance-based optical switching schemes. The broadband switching originates from the material's intrinsic nonreciprocity through optically generated heat currents. Our results establish nonreciprocity as a general principle for deterministically controlling symmetry-broken phases with light.
summary: The researchers demonstrated that an antiferromagnet ($	ext{LiFePO}_4$) can have its magnetic domains deterministically switched simply by shining mid-infrared light from opposite directions. This directional switching, which persists over broad wavelengths, is attributed to the generation of nonreciprocal heat currents, establishing a general principle for light control in symmetry-broken materials.
main_problem: To demonstrate deterministic control over antiferromagnetic (AFM) domains using nonreciprocal heat currents generated by mid-infrared light.
main_result: Nonreciprocal, broadband domain switching was achieved in $	ext{LiFePO}_4$ by pumping from opposite sides, confirming that directional heat current is the key mechanism, rather than specific optical resonances.
method: The study used pump-probe techniques with intense mid-infrared pulses ($\lambda=7-19 \mu	ext{m}$) to induce domain switching in a single crystal of $	ext{LiFePO}_4$, while using visible light for imaging the resulting domain states.
model_or_system: The system is the magnetoelectric antiferromagnet $	ext{LiFePO}_4$, which inherently breaks both space-inversion and time-reversal symmetries. The control mechanism relies on generating nonreciprocal heat currents ($\mathbf{J}_c$) that act as a directional symmetry-breaking field.
key_observables: Domain states ($	ext{L+}$ and $	ext{L-}$), change in transmitted light intensity, and the directionality of the induced heat current.
important_parameters: Mid-infrared wavelength range ($7–19 \mu	ext{m}$); temperature dependence around the Néel temperature ($T_N = 50 	ext{ K}$).
main_assumptions: The switching is primarily mediated by nonreciprocal heat currents ($\mathbf{J}_c$), which reverses sign upon reversing the light propagation direction, overcoming limitations of resonance-based control.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate domain imaging showing $	ext{L+} 	o 	ext{L-}$ switching from one side and $	ext{L-} 	o 	ext{L+}$ from the opposite side. Time-resolved measurements track transient changes linked to heating, and simulations map the direction reversal of the heat current.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical basis (symmetry breaking in AFMs) before presenting experimental evidence: first, demonstrating nonreciprocal switching using mid-IR pulses; second, attributing this effect robustly to broadband heat currents rather than resonances; and finally, ruling out simple directional dichroism mechanisms.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful example of controlling symmetry-broken quantum phases (AFMs) using thermal gradients generated by light, suggesting that nonreciprocity via energy deposition is a general principle applicable across various condensed matter systems.
